weakness: The stack was always built at one hard-coded table spot. With a fixed box standing there, every attempt to put the base block down was refused by the planner ('no plan to pre-place') and the same spot was retried until the time budget ran out (10/10 seeds failed; RoboTwin's expert, which also uses a fixed spot, fails too). Repair exposed two more gaps: a spot that is merely clear is not enough, because the far arm could not reach across the body to spots 16 cm off-centre and spots behind the box made the forearm pass over it; and when the holding arm could not reach the target there was no fallback, so the block was dropped and a failed grasp by the far arm pushed another block off the table.
how_found: Questioned A1 (the build spot is empty). Clutter left exactly where the robot intends to work is the most common surprise on a real table, and the pipeline had no notion of choosing where to work.
why_missed: The task generator keeps that region free of objects, so the hard-coded spot always worked in the nominal scene and reachability by both arms was never in question.
fix: The build spot is now chosen at run time from a grid of table spots: at least 10 cm from the footprint of every perceived object that is not a task block, 12 cm from loose blocks, with a clear straight corridor from both arm bases, ranked by |x| (the far arm reaches across) and then by distance to the preferred spot. While holding the block the pipeline tries the ranked spots in order. If the holding arm reaches none of them, it sets the block down near the middle on its own side and the other arm takes the next try. A grasp the side arm cannot plan is retried with the other arm.
general_rule: Never hard-code where an object should go: choose the goal location at run time from perceived free space, require it to be reachable by every effector that must act there, keep ranked alternatives, and have a fallback (another effector or an intermediate set-down) when the current effector cannot reach.

weakness: The last block stood in a U of three light boxes with 1 cm gaps. The standard grasp picks one top-down wrist angle by preference, its open fingers would land on the boxes, and the planner refused every approach. The pipeline's only remedy for a blocked grasp was to move other task blocks, so it retried the same grasp until the 80 s budget ran out (0/10). Repair exposed two more gaps. With the finger line cleared, the planner's safety padding still refused to descend into the 1 cm gaps beside the fingers. And the extra clearing motions ran out the time budget, because the pipeline re-opened open grippers and re-homed arms that were already parked (1-2 s each).
how_found: Questioned A6'/A14 (only task objects can block a grasp, and some top-down grasp is always free). On a real table, clutter is often packed right against the object you want, and the pipeline had never looked at where its open fingers would go.
why_missed: The task generator keeps the blocks at least 10 cm apart with nothing else on the table, so the default grasp always had free space. The clearing code was written for the only blocking case that had occurred (another block).
fix: Before each grasp, the pipeline checks where the open fingers would land on both face-aligned finger axes, against every perceived object. It picks the axis with the fewest objects in the way and lifts those objects aside, using a manual top-down grasp tried at both wrist directions and setting them down on a free spot. Then it grasps along that axis, letting the final descent touch only neighbours that stand beside the fingers. Gripper and homing motions that would not change anything are skipped.
general_rule: Before grasping, check the space the open gripper will sweep against every perceived object (not just the ones the task names), choose the approach that needs the least clearing, move what is in the way, and accept contact only with neighbours that your own geometry check shows the fingers will clear.

weakness: The build spot was chosen once, at time 0, and reused on every try. A box that slid onto it 2 s later made every attempt to put the base block down fail ('no plan'), and the robot kept retrying the same stale spots until time ran out (s_break 0.3). Repair exposed three more costs. (1) The grasp fallback ladder tried the far arm, and an untilted top-down pose, even where neither can reach, and that burned the 80 s budget. (2) The planner's padded model of the hand refuses to come down within about 6-8 cm of a neighbour, so a contact allowance limited to 3 cm was useless. (3) Allowing contact on free-form or lifting paths let the arm swing through neighbours and fling 10 g blocks off the table.
how_found: Questioned A16 (the scene is static apart from the robot, so a location chosen at the start stays valid). In a shared workspace people put things down while the robot is working, and this pipeline computed its plan only once.
why_missed: Nothing moved in the earlier scenes, so computing the spot once at the start behaved exactly like recomputing it before each use.
fix: The build spot is now chosen right before every placement, from a fresh look. Before choosing, the pipeline waits (at most 3 s) until no perceived object moves more than 1 cm between looks 0.2 s apart. Verification is against the goal actually used. Also: the far arm is not tried for blocks beyond its reach; manual grasps try approaches tilted by 0.35 and 0.6 rad; descents among neighbours allow contact only on a short orientation-locked path; and lifts allow contact with neighbours only if a plain lift has no plan.
general_rule: Choose each goal location from a fresh observation taken immediately before acting on it, after waiting for the scene to stop moving, and never reuse a location chosen earlier in the episode.

weakness: The pipeline checked only the block it had just put down and never re-checked the stack. When the middle block was knocked off after passing its check, the pipeline stacked the top block onto the fallen block lying on the table and declared itself done (0/10). Repair exposed four more problems. (1) After a bump, a block could end up jammed against the hand, every plan from the current pose was refused, and the arm stayed stuck. (2) Without a precondition, most of the time budget went on putting a block onto a support that had just been knocked over; a first, naive precondition check made the two arms hand the block back and forth. (3) Checks with too few samples and a tolerance close to the noise level redid work that was already correct. (4) Every failed grasp variant paid for a lift and a fresh approach, although a refused plan had not moved the arm at all.
how_found: Questioned A17 (a block that passed its check stays put). In a real workspace a finished structure gets bumped by people, by the other arm, or by settling, and the pipeline checked each step once and then forgot it.
why_missed: In the earlier scenes nothing disturbed a finished step, so checking each step once looked sufficient. The cost of a disturbance only appeared when it hit between steps.
fix: The stack is now built in a closed loop. After every step the pipeline waits for the scene to settle and checks every relation of the goal from the bottom up, using 20-sample averages and tolerances inside the task's own. It sets aside anything resting on a misplaced block and redoes the lowest broken level. Before every placement it checks the target's precondition (the stack below is right); if that fails, it puts the held block down out of the way and returns to the loop. A jammed hand is freed by lifting straight up, with contact allowed only near the hand. After a refused plan the pipeline tries the next pose directly, without a lift and a fresh approach.
general_rule: Treat the goal as a set of relations to be re-verified as a whole after every action and before every action that depends on them, and repair the lowest broken relation first, instead of assuming that a step verified once stays done.

weakness: Every way the pipeline knew to free a block assumed it could reach the block from above: lift away whatever crowds it, then grasp top-down. With a fixed slab 1 cm above the block, the pipeline tried to lift the slab (it cannot move), then retried top-down grasps that the slab blocks, and ran out of time (0/10; RoboTwin's expert fails too). Repairs: (1) obstacles that do not rise when lifted are now remembered as immovable; (2) a non-prehensile push with the closed top-down hand did nothing, because a single long move_by was planned over the block rather than through it, and in short increments the palm (about 5 cm above the fingertips) hits the slab edge before the fingers reach the block; (3-4) dragging the block out with a horizontal side grasp works occasionally (best 0.2), but the hand must pass through the 6 cm gap between table and slab. Once the planner's padding is added, that gap is too small for most block orientations.
how_found: Questioned A21 (every block can be reached from above, or made reachable by lifting away what crowds it). Objects under shelves and in cubbies are common on real tables.
why_missed: Every earlier obstruction was beside the target and movable, so lifting it away was always enough. Nothing ever covered a target from above.
fix: Not recovered within the repair budget; the variation is marked unsolved and reverted, and the pipeline is back at its round-4 version. The remaining options (a horizontal or tilted hand in the 6 cm gap) all hit the same limit: the table is always in the planner's collision world with padding, so the pipeline cannot reach that pose reliably. Lessons kept for the harness: test whether an obstruction is movable before planning around moving it; a push needs short straight segments and a pusher whose whole body, not just its tip, clears the space the object leaves.
general_rule: Before planning to move an obstruction, test whether it can move at all, and before relying on a non-prehensile push or a side reach, check that the hand's full body (palm and wrist, not just the fingertips) fits through the space the object occupies, otherwise pick a different strategy early instead of spending the time budget on retries.

weakness: The table top was the only place the pipeline would work. Build and relay spots were always at table height, and every obstacle footprint was off-limits, even blocking the arms' corridors whatever the obstacle's height. With a broad, low, fixed tray filling the middle front of the table, no table spot was reachable by both arms and the relay band was covered. The base block could not be put down, failed placements opened the gripper and dropped blocks from height, and every seed ran out of time (0/10). RoboTwin's expert succeeds, because its fixed target happens to land on the tray top. Repair exposed a second limit: building on a raised surface uses up the arms' vertical reach. The top block of a stack on the 8 cm tray must be released around 1.0 m, at the edge of what a top-down hand can reach away from the body, so its placement often had no plan.
how_found: Questioned A22 (the table top is the only work surface). Real tables carry trays, boxes and books with flat tops, and people build on them all the time. The pipeline only ever looked for free *table*, so a flat obstacle counted purely as a loss of space.
why_missed: There was always free table near the middle, so a stable flat top never had to be considered, and stacks never got high enough to reach the arms' height limit.
fix: Candidate build spots now include the level tops of other objects: the top must be within about 11 deg of level and at least 9 cm wide, and the block centre must sit at least 3.5 cm inside its edges. The corridor check ignores objects lower than the work height (the arms reach over them). Placement allows contact only with the surface the block will rest on. On a raised surface the preferred spot moves towards the robot in proportion to the height, and high targets use a shorter pre-place approach. A block that cannot be placed is put back where it was picked up, instead of being dropped.
general_rule: Treat any stable, level, large-enough surface, not only the table, as a place to work or to hand objects over, but count its height against reach: the higher the work, the closer to the robot and the shorter the approach must be.
